stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, Frebécourt, above the Meuse
stops.campa: Pierre is born in the castle on its lone promontory above the meeting of the Meuse and the Saônelle, the stronghold the bishops of Toul raised and the Brixey lords made their name. His father is Simon, his mother Agnès; the family of Domrémy and the Vosges estate hold lands across France that yield wine, wool and cotton. From the ramparts the valley runs north toward Greux and Domrémy, the villages the house shepherds. In the halls below, music, song and the love-poetry of the troubadours already fill the evenings.

stops.name: Domrémy: the church of Saint-Rémy, the family's village
stops.campa: The boy rides down the valley with his father to Domrémy, where the lords of Bourlémont hold half the village, the church side bounded by the brook. He hears the bell of Saint-Rémy over the roofs and watches the villagers bring their rents of grain and geese. These are his people and this is his ground: the parish whose children his house will shepherd for two centuries more, until a girl of this same street, born the year the male line fails, speaks the name Bourlémont before her judges at Rouen.

stops.name: The beech on the Vaucouleurs road, l'Arbre des Dames
stops.campa: On the hillside where the family lands run toward the Bois Chenu stands the great beech the country calls the Ladies' Tree, with its spring running from the ground beside it. Pierre plays beneath it with the village children, and the old wives already tell the romance of the tree: that a Seigneur Pierre de Bourlémont and a lady called Fée once met and loved beneath these boughs. He carries the name of that lord of the story. The fairies keep the tree; the children dance; the water heals the fevered who believe.

stops.name: Neufchâteau, the fairs of the Meuse
stops.campa: At Neufchâteau, the walled market town an hour's ride south of the castle, Pierre learns the family trade at his father's side: the wool of the Vosges flocks weighed and bargained, the wine of the southern estates rolled off the carts, letters from the Provence cousins read aloud among the bales. Cloth is the house's second dominion, the loom its second sword. The boy watches silver change hands and learns that a bolt of good cloth travels farther than a knight, and that the roads of trade are also the roads of diplomacy.

stops.name: Tarascon, the finca of the Provence branch
stops.campa: Pierre comes south with his father to the finca of the Bourlémont of Provence, the branch of the family grown wealthy in the cloth trade beside the Rhône. Here the salons are never silent: music, singing and the amorous poetry of the troubadours fill every hall of the estate, as they fill all the family haciendas of Provençal culture. And here is his cousin Giovanna, quick-eyed and quicker-tongued, who loves the songs best of all. The two cousins are close from the first summer; the halls belong to them.

stops.name: Beaucaire, the fair across the Rhône
stops.campa: For the feast of the Magdalene the cousins cross the Rhône to the great fair of Beaucaire, where the cloth of Provence meets the merchants of Genoa, Marseille and the Italian towns. Pierre walks the stalls with Giovanna, naming the weaves and the dyes as his father taught him at Neufchâteau; she names the singers. The fair is a whole world laid out on trestles: silks, wool, spice, songs in four languages, and among the Italian cloth-men who come year after year are the traders of Assisi. The river carries everything toward everything.

stops.name: Marseille, embarkation with his father
stops.campa: In spring the mission begins: Pierre's father takes ship at Marseille on an errand of commerce and diplomacy that will carry them to the Caucasus, and the boy goes with him. Bales of Provence cloth are swung aboard as gifts and as samples; letters of credit and letters of courtesy travel in the same casket. Pierre stands at the rail as the Vieux Port opens onto the sea, a child of the Meuse learning the salt of the world. The journey east will make him; he will spend his manhood trying to give it away.

stops.name: Constantinople, the Golden Horn
stops.campa: The ship passes under the walls of Constantinople and into the Golden Horn, and Pierre sees the greatest city of the world stacked in gold and smoke above the water. In the quarters of the Latin merchants his father trades cloth and gathers intelligence for the road ahead; the boy gapes at Haghia Sophia and at emperors carved in porphyry. Here the West thins out and the East begins: caravans, interpreters, coins with unreadable faces. He learns his first words of Greek and his first lesson of diplomacy: listen longer than you speak.

stops.name: Trebizond, the gate of the mountain roads
stops.campa: From the Black Sea the travelers land at Trebizond, where the mountains stand up behind the town and the caravan roads climb toward Armenia, Georgia and the lands of the Kura. The cloth is loaded onto mules; the sea-legs are traded for saddle-sores. Pierre rides among drovers and monks and silk-men, hearing the languages change at every pass. His father tells him the names of the kingdoms ahead and the courtesies each expects. The boy keeps a wooden tablet of new words, the first cipher of his life.

stops.name: Tiflis, the Kura road into Arran
stops.campa: The caravan comes down to Tiflis on the Kura, where the Georgian kingdom glitters between the mountains and the baths steam under the fortress. Pierre's father pays the courtesies of a passing envoy; the boy watches falcons flown from gloved fists and hears psalms sung in a tongue older than Latin. Then the road bends southeast, following the great river down into Arran, the country of orchards and silk between the Kura and the Araxes. Somewhere ahead, in a city of poets, an old master is waiting whom neither of them has heard named.

stops.name: Ganja, arrival at the court
stops.campa: Father and son ride into Ganja on the Ganjachay, the city of gardens and poets in the country of Arran, and are received at court on their errand of commerce and diplomacy. The bales of Provence cloth are unrolled before connoisseurs of silk; the letters of courtesy are read; the mission is welcomed for the winter. Pierre, a French boy in a Persian court, is a wonder to the courtiers and they to him. In this city lives Nizami, the poet who never leaves it, whose verses the whole East carries away instead.

stops.name: Ganja: Nizami takes a liking to the young Frank
stops.campa: Nizami likes Pierre Bourlémont. The master who refuses every sultan's invitation makes room at his side for a merchant's boy from France, and through the winter they read together the stories of the Shahnameh of Ferdowsi: the Age of Heroes, kings and paladins and the long war of Iran and Turan. The poet unrolls the verses; an interpreter carries them across; the boy leans in until he needs the interpreter less. What passes between them is not trade and not diplomacy but the third thing both serve: the story that outlives the road.
